nodes.title: HET-s fibrils
nodes.body:
Struts
A fungal prion that folds into a very stable, ordered fibre. Each fibre is a strut of the gel, with a desthiobiotin handle on its ends.
nodes.name: HET-s fibrils

nodes.title: Tetrahedral streptavidin nodes
nodes.body:
Nodes
Each node has four binding pockets, so it joins four struts. The length of strut between nodes sets the pore size.
nodes.name: Tetrahedral streptavidin nodes

nodes.title: Free biotin releases the gel
nodes.body:
Switch
Biotin outcompetes desthiobiotin for the nodes, so the network comes apart on command and the gel can be cleared or reused.
nodes.name: Free biotin releases the gel

nodes.title: Project description
nodes.body: We build a protein hydrogel from HET-s prion fibrils joined by engineered protein nodes, so the gel has an ordered structure, tunable pores and a switch that takes it apart. [Draft copy]
nodes.name: Project description

nodes.title: Why current hydrogels fall short for enzyme work
nodes.name: Why current hydrogels fall short for enzyme work

nodes.title: Synthetic gels
nodes.body: Built from organic monomers, they are strong and stable, but hard to degrade and poorly biocompatible. Their networks are disordered, which limits how well they can hold enzymes in industrial settings.
nodes.name: Synthetic gels

nodes.title: Protein gels
nodes.body: Gentler on cells and easy to break down, protein hydrogels are growing in drug delivery, tissue engineering and biocatalysis. They are often mechanically fragile and lack an ordered structure.
nodes.name: Protein gels

nodes.title: Our answer
nodes.body: We use amyloid as the building block, because it brings strength and order. HET-s folds into a dense β-solenoid with extensive hydrogen bonding. It is a functional prion and not a pathogen.
nodes.name: Our answer

nodes.title: A structured gel that comes apart
nodes.body:
Goal one
A network with three or more nodes that can be taken apart without harsh solvents such as 1 M NaOH.
nodes.name: A structured gel that comes apart

nodes.title: Enzymes held at standard conditions
nodes.body:
Goal two
Functional enzymes immobilised on the gel at ordinary conditions, so they can be reused. Our dry lab builds a virtual toolbox in parallel, to predict how gel strength, polymerisation and structure respond to design choices.
nodes.name: Enzymes held at standard conditions

nodes.title: 1. Give HET-s an end handle
nodes.body: Wild-type HET-s has no cysteines, so an engineered cysteine is a convenient place to attach something. A maleimide-PEG-desthiobiotin linker reacts with it, and the PEG spacer keeps desthiobiotin reachable by the node.
nodes.name: 1. Give HET-s an end handle

nodes.title: 2. Grow struts of a chosen length
nodes.body: Pre-formed fibrils are the struts. Fibril length between nodes sets the pore size, and the dry lab model predicts which rates and construct ratios give useful lengths.
nodes.name: 2. Grow struts of a chosen length

nodes.title: 3. Join them with nodes
nodes.body: Tetrahedral streptavidin-based nodes bind the desthiobiotin ends. Streptavidin keeps strong binding with a slow dissociation rate, which makes the crosslinks stable.
nodes.name: 3. Join them with nodes

nodes.title: 4. Attach proteins with sortase A
nodes.body: Every HET-s monomer carries an N-terminal LPETG motif. Enhanced sortase A ligates any protein with an N-terminal glycine tag to it. GFP goes first, because it gives a simple readout.
nodes.name: 4. Attach proteins with sortase A

nodes.title: 5. Release the gel on command
nodes.body: Free biotin outcompetes desthiobiotin, saturates the nodes and releases the crosslinks. Sonication or vortexing then breaks up the remaining fibrils.
nodes.name: 5. Release the gel on command

nodes.title: Three strategies for placing cysteines at the fibril ends
nodes.body: Labelling the body of a fibril would tangle the network, so we test three construct strategies in parallel. Each one aims to leave cysteines reachable only at the two fibril ends. All constructs share a C-terminal polyhistidine tag for Ni-NTA purification and an N-terminal LPETG motif.
nodes.name: Three strategies for placing cysteines at the fibril ends

nodes.title: Three-construct capping
nodes.body:
Strategy 1
A tetrameric seed with an N-terminal cysteine starts growth and marks one end. Unmodified HET-s fills the middle. An engineered cap with a C-terminal cysteine and a shortened half unit blocks growth at the other end.
nodes.name: Three-construct capping

nodes.title: Two-construct buried cysteine
nodes.body:
Strategy 2
One cysteine sits inside the solenoid-forming region, so it is buried in the fibril and exposed only at one end. The opposite end is capped as in strategy 1, and this strategy needs fewer constructs.
nodes.name: Two-construct buried cysteine

nodes.title: One construct, two buried cysteines
nodes.body:
Strategy 3
A single protein carries two cysteines near the N and C ends of the solenoid, buried along the body and reachable at both ends, so it needs no cap.
nodes.name: One construct, two buried cysteines

nodes.title: Two case studies for the gel
nodes.name: Two case studies for the gel

nodes.title: A cellulosome mimic
nodes.body:
Case study one
Breaking cellulose down to glucose needs endoglucanases, cellobiohydrolases (CBH) and β-glucosidase (BG). We scaffold CBH and BG together on the gel. CBH makes cellobiose, which also inhibits CBH, so BG has to clear it fast.
The natural cellulosome does this by holding the two enzymes close together, which has been measured to speed up breakdown by up to four-fold. We test whether our fibril and node layout can copy that effect with entirely different chemistry.
• The BG is a glucose-tolerant variant (T. reesei Cel1A L167W/P172L), so the node keeps working as glucose builds up.
• Glucose released over time is read with a GOPOD assay and compared against free enzymes.
• The four-fold figure is a literature benchmark, not a result we expect to repeat.
nodes.name: A cellulosome mimic

nodes.title: A CotA laccase gel
nodes.body:
Case study two
Bacterial CotA laccase uses four copper ions to oxidise many dyes and pollutants. Free laccase degrades quickly and is hard to recover from effluent. Held on the gel, it can be reused.
The β-sheet surface of amyloid fibrils may also pull aromatic pollutants close to the enzyme, through hydrophobic contacts, hydrogen bonds and π-π stacking.
• CotA is expressed in E. coli with CuSO4 in the medium, so the copper centre forms.
• Water with malachite green runs through the gel. The dye bleaches to colourless, and absorbance gives the catalytic efficiency.
• The gel could carry copper and shed fragments into the effluent, so our biosecurity framework asks every user to characterise their discharge.
nodes.name: A CotA laccase gel

nodes.title: ThT anisotropy
nodes.body: At pH 7, HET-s fibrils bind Thioflavin T without the usual jump in fluorescence. Bound dye tumbles slowly, so polarisation rises instead. We follow that signal for lag time, half time and elongation rate.
nodes.name: ThT anisotropy

nodes.title: Negative-stain TEM
nodes.body: It gives a fast first look at fibril length and shape, resolving points 1 to 2 nm apart. It shows the whole structure, while a dye only reports β-sheet.

nodes.title: Model
nodes.body: Our dry lab asks how long the fibrils will be and how large the pores will be, two questions the wet lab cannot answer quickly. Two models work together to answer them. [Draft copy]
nodes.name: Model

nodes.title: Aggregation, fragmentation and decay
nodes.body: Classic prion models track total mass and concentration. We track every fibril length separately, so we can predict the whole length distribution, which is what sets pore size.
nodes.name: Aggregation, fragmentation and decay

nodes.title: The approach
nodes.body:
The model starts from the population balance framework of Goriely and colleagues, closely related to Smoluchowski’s theory of particle coagulation. A state vector holds the concentration of every i-mer, from monomers up to the largest fibril the system can contain, and total mass is conserved.
Our addition is a size-dependent collision kernel, built to capture more of the thermodynamics and kinetics, filled with data and checked against measured size distributions over time.
nodes.name: The approach

nodes.title: One equation, four processes
nodes.body:
∂cᵢ/∂t = Dᵢ Δ cᵢ + Nᵢ + Aᵢ − Fᵢ
The change in the number of i-mers is set by diffusion, nucleation, aggregation and fragmentation. Diffusion uses a cylindrical geometry for a tube of solution, with length-dependent friction from the Tirado theory for rod-like molecules.
nodes.name: One equation, four processes

nodes.title: Formation of new fibrils
nodes.body:
Nucleation
In primary nucleation, k₁ monomers join at once. In secondary nucleation, monomers join on the surface of an existing fibril.
nodes.name: Formation of new fibrils

nodes.title: Joining of fibrils
nodes.body:
Aggregation
Cᵢ + Cⱼ → Cᵢ₊ⱼ
The process is symmetric, and a correcting function sets how likely each pair is to stick.
nodes.name: Joining of fibrils

nodes.title: Breaking of fibrils
nodes.body:
Fragmentation
A larger fibril has to catalyse each break. Breaks caused by heat are left out on purpose.
nodes.name: Breaking of fibrils

nodes.title: Movement in solution
nodes.body:
Diffusion
Diffusion follows the Stokes-Einstein relation and slows as a fibril gets longer.
nodes.name: Movement in solution

nodes.body: The section on the collision-aggregation correcting function α is still to be written. [In progress]
nodes.name: text

nodes.title: Molecular dynamics of the hydrogel
nodes.body: Mesh size is the distance between neighbouring crosslinks. For an enzyme-loaded gel the pores must be smaller than the enzyme, so it cannot leak, and large enough for substrate and product to pass. Measuring mesh size in the lab needs swelling tests, rheology, scattering or NMR, all of which use scarce gel and lab time.
nodes.name: Molecular dynamics of the hydrogel

nodes.title: Why not a simple geometry model?
nodes.body: A random cylinder model predicted alginate mesh size well (R² above 0.95). Alginate consists only of linear chains, while ours has rigid fibrils, elastic PEG linkers and nodes whose binding is dynamic, so a static geometric model would not be reliable.
nodes.name: Why not a simple geometry model?

nodes.title: Why HOOMD
nodes.body: HOOMD-blue defines rigid bodies, flexible molecules and binding potentials, and runs coarse-grained models on GPUs. MARTINI and CHARMM are too fine-grained and LAMMPS is less flexible. It also works with Fresnel for visualising the result.
nodes.name: Why HOOMD

nodes.title: Implicit solvent
nodes.body: The model does not draw water molecules, and a Bussi thermostat holds the system at constant temperature in an NVT ensemble, and effective potentials stand in for solvent effects.
nodes.name: Implicit solvent

nodes.title: A rigid helix of spheres
nodes.body:
Fibril
A union of spheres matching the HET-s fibril diameter, with cut-off Lennard-Jones collisions.
nodes.name: A rigid helix of spheres

nodes.title: PEG modelled as beads
nodes.body:
Linker
One bead per repeat unit, using the coarse-grained parameters of Prasitnok and Wilson.
nodes.name: PEG modelled as beads

nodes.title: A core sphere with four binding sites
nodes.body:
Node
A central sphere with four small spheres on its surface. Only those four bind biotin strongly.
nodes.name: A core sphere with four binding sites

nodes.title: Two ways to measure mesh size
nodes.body:
Read-out
End-to-end distance between nodes, tied to swelling and elastic modulus, and a pore size distribution from an image distance transform.
nodes.name: Two ways to measure mesh size

nodes.title: A functional prion
nodes.body:
Not infectious
HET-s mediates heterokaryon incompatibility in the fungus Podospora anserina. It has no homology to the human prion protein and no route of transmission to mammals, and its sequence is already published.
nodes.name: A functional prion

nodes.title: A purified product
nodes.body:
Cell-free
The product is purified protein, made of HET-s struts, nodes and enhanced sortase A. Engineered organisms are needed only for production and never leave the lab, which removes the risks of environmental release and horizontal gene transfer.
nodes.name: A purified product

nodes.title: A designed off-switch
nodes.body:
Off-switch
Biotin outcompetes the desthiobiotin linker and the network comes apart. Disassembly is still a proof-of-concept endpoint, so our framework asks for efficiency, residual fibril content and time to inactivation to be reported.
nodes.name: A designed off-switch

nodes.title: Fibrils survive autoclaving
nodes.body: HET-s fibrils resist protease and heat, so a standard autoclave cycle is not a reliable way to decontaminate them. The framework asks for a defined waste route in every distributed protocol.
nodes.name: Fibrils survive autoclaving

nodes.title: Checking for residual nickel
nodes.body: We purify with His-tags on Ni-NTA. A team at the Mini Jamboree raised nickel leaching from immobilised laccase. Our sortase-based immobilisation carries no metal chelate into the final material, but we added a residual nickel check to our roadmap, and would move to a FLAG tag if it matters.
nodes.name: Checking for residual nickel

nodes.body: While training us on large-capacity centrifuges, Elizabeth McCormack helped us notice that mismatched Nalgene and Beckman tubes were stored together in a communal container, which risks an unbalanced rotor. We sorted them, for everyone who uses the lab.

items.title: Sir Paul Nurse
items.body:
Nobel laureate, Director of the Francis Crick Institute
Wet Lab

About them
Sir Paul Nurse is a geneticist and cell biologist who was awarded the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discoveries in cyclin-dependent regulation of the cell cycle. He is Director of the Francis Crick Institute and a former President of the Royal Society. Sir Paul is also a popular science writer; in 2020, he published a book What is life? in which he explores the concept of being alive, separating biology into five fundamental pillars and interweaving the narrative with personal experiences.

Why we asked
Imperial College London hosts an annual Sir Ernst Chain Lecture celebrating Imperial’s work in life sciences and the contributions of Sir Ernst Chain to advancing humanity’s knowledge. Sir Paul Nurse was hosting the annual lecture this year. Seeing this event as an opportunity to chat with Sir Paul about our project and get his insights on scientific communication, we quickly signed up for the event. Beyond the chance to be inspired, we hoped to hear how one of the most influential figures in modern science, a Nobel laureate whose career has been defined by both rigorous research and public advocacy for science, would approach the challenge of communicating contested science, such as a prion-based material, to the public.

The conversation
After introducing reGELerate to Sir Paul, we asked him what he saw as the best strategy for lifting the stigma off revolutionary yet shunned areas of science, including genetic engineering and prion translation to biomaterials. His answer focussed on citizenship education, which we interpreted as the need to prepare the society, particularly its members not pursuing a scientific career, to make critical decisions about new science. Sir Paul stated that responsible citizens need to understand what science is, how it works, and why it is a reliable tool for generating knowledge. If people truly understand the scientific process, they will be able to trust it and distinguish good science from malpractice and misinformation.

He suggested that this message, the idea of science as a reliable tool for knowledge production, must be interweaved into our scientific communication. When presenting a project, he recommended explaining not only its purpose and application but also why the science behind it generates knowledge people can trust.

One last piece of advice Sir Paul gave us is to be sceptical of our own ideas. He suggested that excessive self-trust is a barrier in science. Rather than having a good idea and seeking support for it, scientists should constantly “attack” this idea until its reliability is clear.

What it changed
Sir Paul’s advice was broad but foundational to how we approached scientific communication in our project. We applied that very same scrutiny he strongly endorsed to our communication by always highlighting the weaknesses of our product or aspects we did not consider alongside its changemaking potential. Looking at this as our first Integrated Human Practices interaction from the endpoint of our project, we are also implementing the same philosophy into our wiki writing. We are describing our science honestly and clearly, being explicit about our work’s limitations and letting the readers judge for themselves whether the knowledge we produced is reliable and to what extent.

His call for self-scepticism also resonated with our lab practice. We sought to challenge our own interpretations, using negative controls and cross-validating results between methods, as when an unexpected NMR time course was checked against negative-stain EM. Finally, his emphasis on teaching the value of the scientific method in generating reliable knowledge, rather than only its facts, reinforced the approach of our school workshops and other educational resources. When giving presentations about synthetic biology, we always discussed the challenges faced by the field around public mistrust and the steps that need to be taken to gain trust. We explained not only the surface of the science but the journey one needs to take to demonstrate its reliability and true societal value.

items.title: Dr Reed Wickner
items.body:
Geneticist and prion biologist, discoverer of yeast prions
Wet Lab

About them
Dr Reed Wickner is a prominent geneticist and prion biologist based in Maryland, USA. Through his rigorous work, Dr Wickner made multiple foundational discoveries, including the discovery of yeast prions. Namely, his group demonstrated that the [URE3] and [PSI] non-Mendelian genetic elements act as infectious prions in yeast. Dr Wickner has also worked closely with Dr Robert Tycko and other researchers involved in the resolution of the HET-s functional prion crystal structure through solid-state NMR. Finally, Dr Wickner created a dynamic cloud model for prions, pinpointing how they tend to exist as multiple structural variants, displaying conformational diversity.

Why we asked
After the consensus was reached to work with prions, we were particularly fascinated by their structural robustness and saw potential in biomaterials. Initially, we considered Ure2p and Sup35p proteins, encoded by the [URE3] and [PSI] elements, respectively. However, Dr Wickner’s dynamic cloud model raised concerns for reproducibility and reliability of such a project. Of course, in a robust and programmable biomaterial, which we intended, the lack of conformational uniformity would cause severe issues; it would prevent us from reliably designing constructs that form different components of the hydrogel and effectively synergise together. For this reason, we were considering the HET-s functional prion, an exception from the dynamic cloud model, existing in a single conformation, as a primary candidate. We wanted to appeal to Dr Wickner’s expertise to understand whether HET-s, which would form the very foundation of our project, was the right choice. Finally, we were keen on understanding the nuances of wet lab work with HET-s. With our PI having previously been in contact with Dr Wickner, we quickly put our foot in the door.

The conversation
We had a very profound conversation with Dr Wickner, which lasted nearly two and a half hours. We introduced our project to him and immediately received a confirmation for HET-s. Dr Wickner told us that this prion exists as a homogeneous mixture of structural variants, hence its sharp solid-state NMR structure. When we described our idea as a “self-healing” hydrogel, relying on the aggregational capabilities of prions, Dr Wickner highlighted that such a description may be inaccurate and unfeasible. He suggested that if filaments were to be broken, they would not rejoin end-to-end. Furthermore, “healing” would be difficult to validate experimentally. When discussing the experimental approach, beginning with design and purification of prionic constructs, Dr Wickner suggested using a denaturant to prevent fibrillation.

What it changed
Our conversation with Dr Wickner set a strong tone for the rest of our Integrated Human Practices programme. We realised how valuable a simple conversation can be: we set out with a specific goal when reaching out to him and achieved exactly what was intended. Following Dr Wickner’s approval of HET-s, we designed multiple versions of this prion to act as distinct hydrogel components: a tetramer seed, cysteine mutants, and cap variants. We dropped the headline “self-healing hydrogel” and decided to explain the gel’s intended property as “self-assembly via monomer addition” moving forward. Dr Wickner’s advice on purification methods led us to select guanidine hydrochloride as a potent denaturant for effective extraction of our constructs and reach out to multiple potential sponsors seeking this reagent, ultimately securing a sponsorship from Professor Steve Matthews, who went on to become our secondary PI.

items.title: Prof. Mark Howarth
items.body:
Professor, protein technologies, University of Cambridge
Wet Lab

About them
Professor Mark Howarth is Cambridge University researcher working on Innovating Protein Technologies for Therapeutics and Vaccine Design. Professor Howarth has a synthetic biology background and has developed multiple click biology tools in his lab, including the SpyTag/SpyCatcher system and traptavidin. He advised multiple iGEM teams in the past.

Why we asked
We approached Professor Howarth at a crossroads between two possible enzyme immobilisation strategies: Sortase A technology and the SpyTag/SpyCatcher system. We wanted to understand what the advantages and disadvantages of both are, using his prominent expertise in click biology, and use this knowledge to guide our final choice, defining the backbone of the project’s applicational component.

The conversation
We compared SpyTag/SpyCatcher with Sortase A, explaining our goal to immobilise enzymes on a hydrogel matrix. He strongly advocated for SpyTag/SpyCatcher over Sortase A: lower concentration, insertable into multiple parts of the protein sequence, and the strength of the interaction. When we were discussing reversibility, Professor Howarth explained that SpyTag and SpyCatcher form an irreversible covalent bond. However, he proposed two walkarounds: 1) Engineering protease cleavage sites in the SpyTag/SpyCatcher pair to break the bond, and 2) Using SpyTag-DA and SpyCatcher-EQ mutants which form a strong non-covalent linkage. Albeit, such options only offer single-time reversibility.

We continued the discussion, touching upon resilience and the large size of SpyCatcher raising questions about steric hindrance. Professor Howarth reassured us that steric clash is not an issue in most cases and exemplified the system’s resilience by referencing Professor Neel Joshi’s work combining Curli fibres with SpyTag/SpyCatcher and using the system for enzyme immobilisation. Professor Howarth also raised concerns that using a PEG linker limits our hydrogel’s scalability due to the sheer cost of the sheer reagent and suggested considering a genetically encoded alternative.

What it changed
Professor Howarth offered us a fair evaluation of the two enzyme immobilisation methods. Based on his guidance and our research, we decided to select Sortase A due to greater simplicity, given our short wet lab timeline, as well as more flexible reversibility. We chose Sortase A because SpyTag/SpyCatcher did not offer multiple-round reversibility, which would be important for our platform. Namely, we would want a platform with enzymes removable and reattachable on demand. Looking back on this decision from the final stretch of the project, we stand by prioritising reversibility, since Professor Howarth’s workarounds did not offer multi-round enzyme swapping. We were wrong, however, to describe enhanced Sortase A as the simpler option, as it requires a separately purified enzyme and a large excess of the ligation partner, and Professor Howarth's warning about a high working concentration stood when we received low efficiency data in our enzyme immobilisation assays. With more time, we would adopt a hybrid approach, using SpyTag/SpyCatcher for the permanent fibril-node junctions in place of the PEG linker, while continuing to develop efficient reversible chemistry for the swappable enzyme layer. We have incorporated this into our project roadmap.

items.title: Prof. Salvador Ventura
items.body:
Professor, functional prions and amyloids
Wet Lab

About them
Professor Salvador Ventura leads one of the most established laboratories working on functional prions, amyloids, and protein aggregation. In 2018, he published a paper on the potential of prions in biomaterials and nanotechnology. He specifically worked with HET-s and its applications in hydrogels.

Why we asked
Seeing that Professor Ventura’s research aligns so closely to our work, we wanted to ask for his opinion on our wet lab work and the project overall. As an expert in the field, we wanted to ask him about key gaps, both in wet lab work and dry lab modelling. We were also curious to understand his opinion on the best applications for prion-based hydrogels and on regulatory hurdles with such materials.

The conversation
Our conversation with Professor Ventura ended up being the most critical and insightful integrated human practices interaction we had. He immediately challenged the novelty of our concept, as he has previously seen and himself was involved in functional prion nanomaterials being combined with enzyme immobilisation. He cited work creating a glucose biosensor, antibody-binding fibrils, SpyTag functionalisation, conductive nanowires, and others. He advised us to sell the application over the platform and avoid boldly overstating the novelty of the matrix itself. His advice extended into intellectual property, as the material itself was not necessarily novel, nor patentable, even with caveats of using new HET-s constructs and specific methods of cross-linking, such as PEG-biotin click chemistry. Instead, Professor Ventura suggested focusing intellectual property and marketing efforts on our application(s). He saw the novelty of using Sortase A, as this has not been previously done in the field.

Professor Ventura also made multiple technical notes: HET-s nucleation by design is already efficient and he did not see a point in using a tetramer seed construct. Moreover, he was concerned with normalisation of fibril lengths through simply manipulating stoichiometry, terminus-only functionalisation with Sortase A being insufficient, and enzyme immobilisation potentially altering fibrillation patterns. He also stated that HET-s fibrils disassemble at low pH, with HET-s subunits changing morphology. For protein aggregation modelling, Professor Ventura claimed it would be erroneous to assume the same prediction would apply not only to other protein classes but even to other functional prions. For hydrogel characterisation, he recommended TEM, followed up by AFM and SEM. We also asked Professor Ventura about scale-up; he told us that there has not yet been a technology transfer for prion-based biomaterials, with production being a leading barrier, not stigma or regulatory challenges (though still important). He pushed against using Komagatoella phaffii, since E. coli is cheaper and sufficient. He did believe K. phaffi would be a feasible chassis to express the protein but was once again concerned with costs.

What it changed
Firstly, we decided to reframe the way we communicate our project, shifting away from claiming the novelty of the hydrogel matrix itself and being more conservative about the direct applications of the HET-s-based protein aggregation model. We decided to put more emphasis on Sortase A-based applications in this context, an unexplored niche. We also fed this into our Intellectual Property strategy. We kept in the back of our mind Professor Ventura’s guidance against the tetramer seed construct and, after wet lab testing of the three-construct model involving the seed against the two other (two- and one-construct) models, ruled it out…[FINISH]

We used Professor Ventura’s advice for measurement techniques, heavily relying on TEM to attempt hydrogel characterisation.

Professor Ventura’s advice contradicted that of Dr Noah Sprent regarding K. phaffi. We want to explore mass-scale E. coli fermentation as a scale-up option, however, are not ruling out this yeast, as costs heavily rely on supply chains and only doing more work with nfin bio would enable us to understand whether K. phaffi is a cost-effective option or not. Of all barriers, Professor Ventura highlighted cost as the primary culprit to technology transfer failures, leading us to prioritise cost-effective scale-up in our project roadmap. Lastly, his statement about HET-s defibrillation at low pH offered us a new route for scaffold disassembly on demand which we did not previously consider.

items.title: Dr Freya Leif
items.body:
Field Application Scientist, BMG Labtech
Wet Lab

About them
Dr Freya Leif is a Field Application Scientist at BMG Labtech, a manufacturer of microplate readers. She supports researchers in setting up and optimising assays on BMG instruments.

Why we asked
BMG Labtech loaned us a plate reader, and Dr Leif helped us install it and arranged the loan of two fluorescence polarisation (FP) filter sets: 482-16 / LP504 / 530-40 for AF488 and 450-10 / LP468 / 480-10 for Thioflavin T. BMG also very generously donated flat-bottom black 96-well plates for our assays. After running some initial experiments, we reached back out to Dr Leif for advice on optimising our fluorescence polarisation assays.

The conversation
We first discussed the benefits of fluorescence polarisation as a technique for monitoring binding and assembly when no dye directly reports on the process. FP measures how freely a fluorophore tumbles in solution. A small, free dye rotates quickly and gives a low polarisation signal, while a dye attached to a large, slow-moving structure such as a fibril gives a high one.

Dr Leif then advised us on controls. To establish the dynamic range of each experimental setup, we should measure a negative control of free AF488 in fibril growth buffer, which gives the lowest polarisation, and a positive control of labelled preformed fibrils, which gives the highest. Finally, she explained how to set the gain: calibrate it on the reference well to a target of 35 mP (millipolarisation units), then keep the gain settings fixed for both the parallel and perpendicular channels across all measurements, so that readings remain directly comparable.

What it changed
With properly calibrated gain and defined controls, we could reliably compare our different cysteine mutants by FP. In particular, we could test our expectation that the N-terminal tail mutant, where the dye sits on a more conformationally flexible region, would show a smaller FP change than our backbone mutant. In the backbone mutant, the dye should be held more rigidly once incorporated into fibrils, yielding a higher FP dynamic range.

items.title: Anonymous researcher (Dr A.)
items.body:
Synthetic biology researcher (anonymous)
Wet Lab

About them
This researcher preferred to remain anonymous. Their background lies in synthetic biology, with multiple publications on hydrogels. For the sake of this written piece, we will be referring to this researcher as Dr A.

Why we asked
Early into our project, wanted to sharpen the wet lab component of our project, including applications and the design of hydrogel components, and to get a glance at useful measurement techniques applicable to our context. For this reason, we consolidated Dr A., whose rich scientific background smoothly aligned with our work.

The conversation
We met Dr A. twice, once at an early stage of our project and once right before the beginning of our wet lab component.

During the first meeting, we pitched our initial wet lab idea to Dr A. They believed that a monolayer gel was unlikely to have the sufficient structural integrity or thickness to be marketable as robust or to be characterised. It would also not be able to perform the intended applications. They therefore encouraged us to consider a multilayer design seriously and understand if our work can be slightly modified to enable this. Another suggestion raised was looking into cross-linking molecules to increase gel stability, echoing our PI’s, Dr Manka’s point.

Dr A also proposed to compare our hydrogel against a synthetic alternative such as a collagen or alginate hydrogel, which would strengthen our applications assessment, and incorporate nanoparticles into the gel as a route to functionalisation.

During the second meeting, we came to Dr A. specifically to get their advice on the PEG linker size. We were seeking out a sponsorship from MedChemExpress who offered linkers, ranging from 2-5 kDa in size. Dr A. Suggested PEG-2K fully extends in water due to its high hydrophilicity, becoming fully accessible for click chemistry reactions with HET-s mutants.

What it changed
Dr A.’s advice was pivotal to our project. It pushed us to work on a multilayer version of our hydrogel, sparking many discussions with Dr Manka and ultimately yielding the solution: a gel with struts and linkers, with enough degrees of freedom to become multilayered. It is after conversing with Dr A we designed the strategy of crosslinking the hydrogel by bonding HET-s fibrils to streptavidin nodes via the biotin-PEG linker. By selecting this design, we effectively killed two birds with one stone, solving the monolayer problem and crosslinking the hydrogel. We later confirmed this crosslinking phenomenon for our single cys mutant via EM. The PEG linker we chose was PEG-2K, as per Dr A.’s insight.
