items.title: Edward You
items.body:
Former FBI WMD Directorate agent, biosecurity governance
Biosecurity

About them
Mr. Edward You is a former Supervisory Special Agent in the FBI’s Weapons of Mass Destruction Directorate and a leading global voice in biosecurity and biotechnology governance. Following an early career trajectory in bench science, progressing through molecular biology to clinical autoimmune research, gene-therapy research and cancer biology exploration at Amgen, Edward You joined the FBI after 9/11. There, he spent 15 years as Supervisor Special Agent in the FBI’s Weapons of Mass Destruction Directorate. Ed first worked as a field agent on counterterrorism within the Joint Terrorism Task Force, focusing on Al-Qaeda investigations and HazMat response, and was subsequently promoted to Washington to lead the Bureau’s biological threat portfolio. In 2009, he organised the FBI’s first synthetic biology conference, gathering two of the most influential cofounders of modern synthetic biology such as Drew Endy, Randy Rettberg and members of the DIY-bio community, which led him to push the FBI to sponsor iGEM for 15 years. Ed was the host of the “Safeguarding Science” workshop at the Grand Jamboree, and at the time of interview, was about to testify before Congress.

Why we asked
In our consultation with Edward You, we focused on exploring how a biosecurity framework for an emerging synthetic biotechnology should be constructed, and on the governance models most likely to succeed as biotechnology becomes increasingly decentralised. We were particularly interested in the notion of biology as an open-source field, with most biological materials occurring naturally and lacking control, as well as progress in the field depending on collaborative exchange and peer review. Mr. You brought a unique dual perspective to this back-and-forth, combining his bench-science background with his fifteen-year career at the FBI to underline the importance of shifting biosecurity discourse beyond over-indexed pandemics and bioterrorism, and towards under-indexed biotechnology as critical infrastructure for agriculture, manufacturing and energy. He underlined the UK’s synthetic biology strategy, which the USA lacks, as a positive example of national foresight, comparable to that of China’s sustained investment in the sector. Mr. You maintained that the monitoring of biosecurity risk across such growing industries is as crucial as it is in the pandemic and bioterrorism domains.

The conversation
The central argument advanced by Mr. You was that biosecurity cannot be governed effectively through top-down regulation alone. Under such a model, international authorities design overarching policies that individual nations are expected to translate into domestic legislation. The primary top-down framework for biological threats is the Biological Weapons Convention, initiated in 1972. He underlined that this approach functions reasonably well for other categories of weapons of mass destruction, particularly nuclear materials, whose massive and highly-visible infrastructure and individual components can be inventoried and controlled. However, he highlighted the open-source nature of biology and the dual-use dilemma as a core obstacle, as beneficial and harmful applications can be generated from identical biological components. In particular, the decentralisation of modern tools such as CRISPR means that meaningful use is now present in small and ordinary commercial laboratories which governments possess limited capacity to track.

items.title: Edward You, continued
items.body:
Instead, Mr. You proposed a community-based model founded on the education and empowerment of as many individuals in society as possible - from students to company presidents. This would ensure that responsibility for preventing misuse is understood rather than delegated. He drew on the white-hat and black-hat notion in cybersecurity in order to argue for the cultivation of ethical practitioners who actively probe synthetic biosystems for vulnerabilities and patch them before malicious actors are able to identify them, rather than allowing those vulnerabilities to be first discovered by those seeking destruction or financial gain. He emphasised this by framing the Hippocratic principle of “do no harm” as fundamentally passive, and argued that biologists require a more active “not on my watch” posture that assumes personal responsibility for identifying areas of potential misuse rather than presuming that someone else will intervene. Most interestingly, Mr. You underlined how this currently operates institutionally in the US, where every FBI field office maintains a trained weapons of mass destruction coordinator tasked with proactively building relationships with local universities, laboratories and even garage DIY-bio spaces, such that a suspicious anthrax case would trigger a parallel law enforcement and public health response and researchers possess an established point of contact rather than general emergency line. By drawing on his engagements with the UK Home Office and Metropolitan Police, he observed that the UK lacks an equivalent structure and identified this as a gap that could be addressed to establish firmer governance models for biotechnological tools.

Mr. You also underlined the value of interdisciplinary composition in biosecurity design, noting that teams that combine biologists, engineers, computer scientists and policy experts are better placed to catch environmental, societal and discriminatory harms that a biology-only team may overlook, a structure recognised by our own iGEM team. He illustrated the consequences of insufficiently granular risk assessment through the H5N1 gain-of-function controversy, in which the best-practice risk mitigation model developed by Wisconsin’s Biosecurity Task Force was flattened into the same controversy as the Erasmus work, producing a one-size-fits all restriction to be applied across two fundamentally different technologies. Ultimately, this forecloses any distinction between the risk severity of the biological agents involved.

What it changed
For our own project, he offered three concrete recommendations: to work to understand the public perceptions of biosecurity risk so that all stakeholders come to a feel a shared responsibility to act as white-hat practitioners, to first define the specific downstream applications of our hydrogel since the application determines both our audience and risk profile, and to engage beneficiary communities before approaching regulators, on the basis that grassroots demand from a legitimate industry provides the leverage and the data needed to shape policy discussions proactively rather than merely reacting to existing rules. These recommendations laid the foundation of our biosecurity framework.

items.title: Henrik Hagemann
items.body:
Entrepreneur, Imperial iGEM 2014 alumnus
Entrepreneurship

About them
Henrik Hagemann is a successful entrepreneur with a bioengineering and iGEM background. He is an Imperial College London alumnus and competed on its behalf in iGEM 2014. Henrik spun out his team’s project, Aqualose, into a company CustoMem, and later, Puraffinity. Puraffinity has now raised over $25 million in funding and designs smart materials to purify water from toxic persistent chemicals, PFAS.

Why we asked
Seeing that Henrik is an Imperial and iGEM alumnus, we believed his perspectives would provide us with valuable insight and that speaking to someone who has treaded a similar path would result in a meaningful interaction. After having spoken to Dr Wickner about the core science behind our project, we wanted to ensure we did not leave the entrepreneurial component of the competition behind. We wanted to learn a lesson about entrepreneurship and commercialisation in the context of our project and, more broadly, from someone who achieved success through years of hard work.

The conversation
We started by hearing about Henrik’s experience, the timeline from Aqualose in 2014 to Puraffinity today. Henrik told us that the process of spinning out such a project into a company would take at least 8-10 years of rigorous work and iteration cycles. He identified one of the main reasons for synthetic biology projects failing beyond iGEM as regulatory hurdles and issues with public/stakeholder acceptance, rather than scientific discrepancies. Henrik attributed this reason to his pivot away from synthetic biology towards chemistry with Puraffinity; synthetic biology relies on standardised parts, which are sensitive to scale-up and often fail when contexts shift towards mass-manufacturing. To our question about reasons for rebranding, Henrik stated that CustoMem restricted the company’s evolution; he explained that Puraffinity focused on solutions. Broad purposeful naming enables Henrik to pivot and take the company in multiple directions in the future. A key piece of advice Henrik gave us was to carefully identify an unmet need, to “create” the necessity for our project. For reGELerate, he explained that there are often cases of over-engineering in materials to achieve robustness, such as the use of the carbon-fluorine bond in PFAS chemicals. At the end, Henrik mentioned the recent Deep Science Ventures toxicity report on chemical contamination which highlights the need for non-oil-based materials, a niche accessible to our project.

What it changed
Henrik’s insights about the real reasons for iGEM projects failing contributed to a change in our thinking: we decided to extend the biosecurity component of our project, taking it beyond our conversation with Edward You to build a biosecurity framework. Additionally, we decided to seek out public opinions, despite our project only affecting members of general public downstream; as a result, we conducted a series of public interviews, which fuelled our biosecurity and bioethics frameworks, enabling us to approach the question of commercialisation more responsibly and take crucial steps towards securing public trust, should reGELerate ever make it outside of iGEM. We realised that “reGELerate” as a name makes the same mistake as CustoMem: it emphasises the “what” over the “why”, clipping our wings. Therefore, in our project commercialisation roadmap we included rebranding as a crucial step. Lastly, we zoomed in on market niche identification, seeking out a conversation with Harry Macpherson, who authored the Deep Science Ventures toxicity report. Henrik kindly connected us to him.

We also invited Henrik to speak at a panel on the future of synthetic biology during our UK/EU Mini Jamboree. Read more here.

items.title: Will Wijnberg
items.body:
Entrepreneur in life sciences start-ups
Entrepreneurship

About them
Will Wijnberg is a leader and an entrepreneur working with life sciences companies and start ups. He has raised nearly $30 million since 2020 across three different ventures, including a UTI diagnostic, a medical device business that recently received FDA clearance and Matoke Holdings, a therapeutics company using reactive oxygen species as an antimicrobial. Will has expertise in consultancy, management and commercialisation.

Why we asked
The more perspectives, the better. We took this approach for our entrepreneurship and commercialisation angle of the project. We wanted to consult Will as a successful an entrepreneur with a life sciences background. Moreover, we found a useful parallel between Matoke Holdings’ product under construction, the polymer matrix (previously publicly viewable on their website). The product is a matrix with immobilised oxidase enzymes, with potential applications in wound treatment.

The conversation
We discussed issues with platform-based technologies. William gave us a useful piece of advice: if no individual application is strongly marketable, one thousand times zero is still zero. Will also suggested that iGEM does not let us reach a product endpoint and that we should focus on listing characteristics required by a potential customer and identifying one or two we could demonstrate/have demonstrated within our project’s timeline. He also usefully framed enzyme immobilisation on Matoke’s polymer matrix as a difficult balance between activity, stability, and cost. For products used by the public, using the therapeutics example, he suggested that a retail cost of about $10 and a production cost of $2-3 is a good ballpark to situate yourself in.

What it changed
There was some overlap in Will’s advice with Rahul Khetan’s, when discussing marketability of a platform technology, which pushed us towards developing the cellulose breakdown application more, as well as developing a second application, involving CotA laccase immobilisation. Previously, we had conversations with our advisor Sabyasachi Banerjee, writing his PhD thesis on laccase-based waste valourisation and optimising laccase purification methods. He prompted us to explore this enzyme more for its commercial value in bioremediation and lignocellulose valourisation. Following Will’s interaction, we decided to further develop this application, chasing the “strongly marketable” context.

We conveyed the exercise proposed by Will, outlining the characteristics required by a potential customer for our hydrogel in a table and selecting ones best represented in our project proxy:

This helped us outline our strengths and focus on them in selling the project. We applied this knowledge in business strategy and presentations about our project in September and beyond.

Will’s point about costs also provoked thought. We were later asked by Saman Khan and John Kelly, our sponsors for the UK/EU Mini Jamboree about the costs of our product and their benchmarking during an informal pitching session. We could not present them with specific numbers. Thinking back to that interaction and our conversation with Will, we estimated costs and included them into our business strategy. While we did not design our product for sales to members of the general public, we applied Will’s advice about a 70-80% profit margin in the biotechnology industry.

items.title: Dr Ali Baghdadi
items.body:
Senior Vice President, Ingram Micro (META)
Entrepreneurship

About them
Dr Ali Baghdadi is Senior Vice President of Ingram Micro and Chief Executive of its Middle East, Turkey and Africa (META) region. Over his career he has built companies across Europe, the USA, the Middle East, Africa and Central Asia, establishing and acquiring over 20 companies in fields including IT, cyber security, artificial intelligence, telecommunications, high-tech services, storage media manufacturing, solar and aviation technology. He founded Appropriate Technology (Aptec) based on work from his PhD at Imperial in the late 1970s, and took on his current role after Aptec was sold in 2012 to Ingram Micro, the world’s largest IT and mobility distributor. In 2021, Imperial College London named him Entrepreneur of the Year. He remains closely involved with the university as an Advisor to the student-led Karman Space Program, a Sponsor of the Data Science Society and a Juror for MBA projects at the Business School.

Why we asked
As a self-guided student project, reGELerate doesn’t fit the conventional structure of a student-led society, which raised practical questions about how to organise our team and fund our work. We wanted to speak to Dr Baghdadi because he combines deep business expertise in deep tech and innovation with direct experience mentoring Imperial student teams. His work with the Karman Space Program (KSP) was especially relevant, as it faces many of the same challenges as an iGEM team.

The conversation
We began by discussing Dr Baghdadi’s career and his experience supporting KSP, which has many parallels to iGEM. On team structure, he stressed using team members efficiently: most tasks should not be done by committee but delegated as individual responsibilities. He also highlighted that student-led projects often create opportunities to spin out companies, complementing academic education with the entrepreneurial and problem-solving skills needed to start new businesses.

On finances, Dr Baghdadi emphasised the importance of proper bookkeeping and accounting to track the flow of funds. As an example, he described the expensing system KSP uses to reimburse students, rather than giving the whole team access to a shared credit card. After our conversation, he followed up with further questions, most importantly on the clarity of our deliverable and how novel our idea was compared with existing projects, which we also incorporated into our work.

What it changed
Dr Baghdadi’s advice shaped both how we organise ourselves and how we approach sponsors. Following his point on delegation, we appointed team leads for Wet Lab, Dry Lab and Human Practices. This was not a chain of command but a division of responsibilities: each task had a clear owner who could direct other members to where they would display their strengths best, while everyone could still contribute across all sub-teams. We also elected an overall team lead to coordinate communication between the sub-teams.

At the time of our meeting, we had no pitch deck aimed at potential wet lab and project sponsors. Afterwards, we prepared sponsor-specific decks and elected a dedicated fundraising lead, and we went on to raise over £5,000 worth of reagents from academic and industry sponsors. His follow-up question on novelty also led us to benchmark our project against past prion-based and biomaterials projects in iGEM, sharpening how we communicate what makes reGELerate distinct.

Finally, our conversation prompted us to think about succession. A recurring struggle for Imperial iGEM is that each team starts from scratch, despite the wealth of institutional knowledge held by PIs and former team members in the wider Imperial SynBio community. In response, we opened lines of communication with Growf, the 2025 Imperial team. While this was helpful, we believe successive teams would benefit far more from greater overlap. To build that continuity, three current members, who sit on next year’s SynBio Society committee, have agreed to onboard the next Imperial iGEM team in late December, passing on the key lessons we learned. We have also ensured to provide the next team with a strong starting foundation by scheduling a high school workshop for February 2027 with Dulwich College and compiling useful resources for iGEM teams on our wiki.

items.title: Dr Ben Reeve
items.body:
Deep tech founder, Puraffinity and Modern Synthesis
Entrepreneurship

About them
Dr Ben Reeve is a deep tech founder, co-founding both Modern Synthesis and Puraffinity, and is a former iGEM team member and supervisor to Imperial iGEM 2024. Modern Synthesis is a London-based biotech company that applies materials science to nanocellulose, a natural polymer produced through fermentation, turning it into a new class of responsible textiles and coatings for fashion, footwear and other uses. Drawing on the UK’s strengths in engineering biology and textile innovation, the company aims to shape the future of materials.

Why we asked
We met Dr Reeve at a SynbiCITE networking event, where he presented on Modern Synthesis. As someone who has been both an iGEM participant and supervisor, and who has gone on to found engineering biology companies, he was well placed to advise us on fundraising from sponsors. His experience bringing a biomaterial to market was also directly relevant to reGELerate, and to the question of where an engineered material like ours could realistically fit within existing industries.

The conversation
We first discussed fundraising: how to approach wet lab sponsors, and what companies look for before sponsoring an iGEM team. Dr Reeve then talked us through Modern Synthesis’s collaboration with the Danish luxury brand Ganni, developing a leather-alternative version of its signature Bou Bag to create an animal- and plastic-free take on one of the brand’s iconic items.

This led to a broader discussion of where innovative synthetic biology companies sit within supply chains that still rely heavily on petrochemicals. Echoing his talk, Dr Reeve explained that a new biomaterial should not try to compete with an entire established supply chain, such as the network of artisanal suppliers serving high-fashion leather. Instead, it can augment a small part of that chain, such as coatings for leather, and still add tremendous value and impact. He also noted that synthetic biology products typically carry higher input costs than their petrochemical counterparts, which are environmentally costly but cheap, so they need to offer high added value to compete.

What it changed
Dr Reeve introduced us to his Puraffinity co-founder, Henrik Hagemann, who became a great supporter of our project, helping with fundraising and joining us as a guest speaker at our UK/EU Mini Jamboree in August.

Our discussion of value also shaped our technical direction. Because synthetic biology solutions must justify their higher costs through the value they add, we focused on immobilising multiple enzymes onto our fibril scaffold, increasing the functionality, and therefore the value, that a single material can deliver.

items.title: Hilary Sherman
items.body:
Senior Scientist, Corning Life Sciences
Commercialisation

About them
Hilary Sherman is a Senior Scientist in the Corning Life Sciences Applications Lab. She has been on Corning Inc’s team for over twenty years. Hilary has spearheaded application development for many of Corning’s products, including none other than Matrigel.

Why we asked
We reached out to Hilary for multiple reasons. The first reason is Corning’s Matrigel is possibly the closest commercial counterpart to our product. While not principally an enzyme immobilisation platform, Matrigel is a textbook example of a commercialised hydrogel, acting as a platform technology rather than being confined to one specific application. We wanted to understand how Matrigel was marketed and commercialised to take inspiration for our project and its applications argument.

Furthermore, we wanted to speak to Hilary as we were fascinated by her position as a Senior Applications Scientist. Hilary’s role is specialised in developing applications for technologies, often after they are developed. Having found ourselves in a similar position, with the core wet lab concept resolved but applications missing, we hoped to consult Hilary’s profound expertise.

The conversation
Hilary described to us the details of her position, including selecting products with substantial commercial potential and designing the simplest possible proof-of-concept studies for them. Hilary defined substantial commercial potential as an application which transcends multiple disciplines, such as organoid culture for Matrigel. When discussing our synthetic hydrogel, she identified ordered and controlled synthetic hydrogels as a gap in the market. Drawing a comparison with Matrigel, Hilary explained that its downside is the lack of standardisation, with unknown ratios of constituent proteins. She mentioned that not all contexts require standardisation and high definition; for our project, she suggested identifying areas where a scaffold with high precision and control is required. Another point of contrast was matrigel not only being a structural component but rather a functioning ECM with signalling cues for cellular positioning. Hilary claimed it is very different to reproduce this complexity in pure synthetic systems. In addition, we discussed that it is much easier for larger companies with high budgets to bring platform-based technologies to market. Such technologies often do not immediately carry noticeably lucrative applications, as with Matrigel which began as a tool to study angiogenesis. Corning could develop Matrigel further instead of discontinuing it due to its already sheer size at the time.

Naturally, we asked Hilary, as an expert in hydrogel commercialisation, which niches she believes would best house well-defined synthetic hydrogels. Her example was translating therapeutic organoids into humans, we still have many undefined components when working with organoids in mice which creates safety concerns for human work. Hilary also defined customisability as a highly demanded product feature, using the ability to tailor microenvironments for specific cell types with variable extracellular matrices as an example.

When discussing applications and introducing our enzyme immobilisation ideas, Hilary believed we may not necessarily need to narrow our applications down to one. Another piece of advice she gave was assessing each candidate market on two axes: size and earning potential. Into that analysis she also suggested incorporating the question “how strongly does the platform differentiate from its commercial counterparts?”. The best case scenario is a smaller market with greater differentiation, rather than a larger market with less distinctiveness. Interestingly, Corning followed its customers discovering new applications for Matrigel and scaled the promising cases.

items.title: Hilary Sherman, continued
items.body:
On market entry strategy for a biotechnology product, Hilary described an approach of placing a product with key opinion leaders, usually academics who can publish protocols. By assisting researchers in solving specific problems with their product (which must work well), Corning gains trust in their product and relies on the researchers’ reputation. She characterised the whole approach as marketing conducted through science rather than advertising.

What it changed
Hilary provided us with a plethora of useful advice, critical toward closing the human practices loop. Firstly, she provided us with a model for market analysis, described above. Hilary made us realise the importance of conveying detailed market analysis before attempting entry. While stakeholders like Henrik Hagemann stimulated us to think about market analysis and niche identification, Hilary’s advice pushed us to think more about a direct commercial evaluation: competition and financial attractiveness. Following this, we assessed the market for enzyme immobilisation platforms using Hilary’s model, which helped us streamline our applications from a commercial standpoint.

Even though Hilary identified a considerable gap in the market filled nicely by defined synthetic hydrogels, we chose to pivot away from commercialising our product as a highly controlled platform technology. We did this for two reasons: 1) Hilary explained to us that there are a lot of valuable complex components and interactions within Matrigel which make it so lucrative to customers. Combined with our own uncertainty about how much control we could demonstrate over our system, with limited literature and limited wet lab time, this steered us away from positioning reGELerate as a reliable and well-defined synthetic scaffold. 2) Hilary mentioned that platform technologies experience more success when developed by large companies who do not require immediate product success as much as smaller companies would. We very much fell into the second group, perhaps even outside it as a start-up. Following Hilary’s praise of customisability, we chose to explore enzyme immobilisation applications further, finding ourselves at a crossroads between the SpyTag/SpyCatcher system and Sortase A. We also chose to invest into multiple applications instead of one, as Hilary insinuated.

One final important takeaway from this conversation for us was entering the market through key opinion leaders. For this reason we researched and reached out to key opinion leaders who may benefit from using our technology in their work, gathering their perspectives. Some examples of said opinion leaders are Mark Howarth, Neel Joshi, and Salvador Ventura. Identifying key opinion leaders became a crucial component of our product roadmap.

items.title: Dr Rahul Khetan
items.body:
Venture capital associate, UCB Ventures
Commercialisation

About them
Dr Rahul Khetan is a venture capital associate at UCB Ventures. He specialises in healthcare and biotechnology, investing into startups and assisting in their commercialisation. Rahul also holds a PhD in biopharmaceutical Informatics and is a former iGEMer, having competed as part of the IIT Delhi Team in 2017.

Why we asked
We reached out to Rahul to consult his expertise working with biotechnology startups and gain his advice for commercialisation. We believed that having competed in iGEM in the past, Rahul would have a better context of our situation than some other VCs. After all, most projects in iGEM are marketed as ready solutions, despite there being insufficient time to complete them. Moreover, we were puzzled by marketing a Foundational Advance project. Though we developed an enzyme immobilisation application, it still felt very broad and dependent on enzymes chosen.

The conversation
We asked Rahul about factors which make an iGEM-based startup attractive to investors. He stated that a successful project must start with early validation, combined by a strong multifaceted team and a clear business plan, from bench to market. Rahul was clear that a platform technology without a defined product is often uninvestable. He recommended choosing one lead product with a defined market and follow-up with additional applications later on and explained that platforms usually revolve around license-based softwares. We thought back to our conversation with Hilary Sherman about Corning's Matrigel, which only had its key organoid applications developed later, acting as a successful example of breadth. Nonetheless, Rahul suggested depth must come first at seed stage, directing 60-70% funding to the lead application and establishing a clear direction. He said that wet lab’s key priority for commercialisation would be benchmarking enzymatic activity on our hydrogel against competitors and observing niches where it excels.

Furthermore, we discussed what a good roadmap implies: efficiency studies, milestone setting, scale-up steps, and regulatory approvals. Rahul supported our decision to work at the protein level rather than with genetic circuits, expecting lower regulatory hurdles. Lastly, we learned from Rahul that seed investors do not expect complete patents, rather a patent strategy. We had considered releasing our protein aggregation model as open-source, with paid licences for commercial users. Rahul called this risky, since a startup cannot afford the legal action needed to enforce licences. Rahul also recommended two generalist funds for future investment: Syncona and Novo Holdings.

What it changed
The insights and follow-up opportunities Rahul gave us were difficult to fit into a short write up. Starting with applications, Rahul’s advice reinforced our commitment to a single well-developed application: cellulose breakdown by CBH and β-glucosidase mimicking a cellulosome. Additionally, we developed an assay to test the enzymes’ immobilisation and activity, an initial binary indication of success.

We also dropped our open-source idea for the dry lab protein aggregation model, as per Rahul’s guidance; instead, we began to consider a licensed software with free academic access. Nevertheless, the most important outcome from this interaction was a bench-to-market roadmap we began rigorous work on. Into it we fed parts of Rahul’s recommended steps and Intellectual Property strategy, mentioned above, and the suggested investment funds to approach. As part of our roadmap work, we mapped our team's strengths and weaknesses on a radar chart. This showed the gaps in our combined skills and helped us outline the profiles of new members we would need. Finally, Rahul’s suggestion to explore scale-up particularly sparked our curiosity and prompted us to meet with Noah Sprent from nfin bio, discussing Komagataella phaffi as a possible chassis for upscaling our construct expression and purification.

items.title: Dr Noah Sprent
items.body:
Co-founder and CTO, nfin bio
Commercialisation

About them
Dr Noah Sprent is a co-founder and CTO at nfin bio, a biomanufacturing company scaling the production of recombinant proteins to bioreactor volumes. He advised last year’s Imperial iGEM team, Growf, and assisted part of their research with equipment and facilities. Dr Sprent is also an Imperial College London alumnus, holding a PhD in synthetic biology.

Why we asked
Following our insightful conversations with Dr Rahul Khetan and Dr Amritpal Singh, we seeked to explore more the scale-up of our project. When considering costs, protein purification was the obvious bottleneck, to build a large quantity of hydrogel products, we would need a well-defined, cheaper and more efficient pipeline of HET-s construct expression and purification. We wanted to speak to Dr Sprent about scale-up options, given the context and scientific backbone of our project. We were particularly interested but not limited to his expertise in Komagataella phaffi, a non-model yeast with emerging applications as a protein expression chassis, thanks to its unique secretion system. K. phaffi is also a chassis for Imperial iGEM 2025, echoing their work.

The conversation
We met Dr Sprent in his lab and received a tour as well as an explanation of nfin bio’s goals and work. We asked Dr Sprent to help us assess the feasibility of using K. phaffi for upscaling HET-s construct expression. Dr Sprent told us that there is a high chance of the expression failing, as HET-s would aggregate, rendering it toxic and unlikely to get secreted. He suggested that certain constructs would be possible to express more efficiently, such as the cap, which does not polymerise. Dr Sprent also recommended exploring whether the HET-s beta-solenoids could be modified to prevent intracellular aggregation or be able to control this process through some form of a switch. He recommended reaching out to Dr James Murray, an expert in protein design and beta-solenoids at Imperial. Finally, he proposed a possible research collaboration. nfin bio uses Pioreactor technology and needs support testing certain protocols with them as well as understanding the useful functions. We could test our construct expression in K. phaffi with such a reactor, whilst simultaneously supporting nfin bio’s research, two birds with one stone. A specific assay Dr Sprent suggested within the timeframe of the project was generating a kill curve. This would help us understand whether K. phaffi is a feasible chassis for some of our constructs or if said constructs are toxic to it. More specifically, we would measure OD600 of the wildtype or transformed K. phaffi culture over time, with wildtype HET-s, HET-s constructs and a fluorescent marker, such as RFP, assessed. Dr Sprent suggested that such a binary test is the most important, if expression works, K. phaffi will likely be able to achieve a greater and more cost-effective yield.

What it changed
As our interaction with Dr Sprent happened toward the end of the wet lab timeline, we unfortunately did not have time to actually do the proposed experiment. It would require redesigning some of our constructs for K. phaffi and exploring the beta-solenoid modification, which we could not accommodate the time for.

Something we did gain out of this interaction is a clearer resolution of our scale-up strategy, viewable on our wiki. We generated kill curve predictions, outreach drafts, and codon-optimised some of our constructs for K. phaffi.

On scale-up.

We have an experiment conceptualised to validate the use of K. phaffi as a possible scale-up chassis. Namely, we would test viability over time for K. phaffi cultures expressing our constructs.

items.title: Dr Noah Sprent, continued
items.body:
We generated generalised kill curve predictions, following our discussion with Noah Sprent and would expect similar results to initially validate K. phaffi as a chassis. In case of successful validation and tolerance to HET-s construct(s), we would then compare the yield from protein purification and estimate the cost per milligram.

To further facilitate this experiment in the future, we codon-optimised three of our chief constructs, wildtype HET-s, tetramer seed and 1.5-unit HET-s cap, for the pPICZα A vector K. phaffi, using the Benchling codon optimisation tool. We ensured these optimised constructs are RFC[10]-compatible. They can now be ordered and tested in vitro. Since we did not yet test these constructs, we did not add them to the iGEM Registry of Standard Biological Parts.

We also drafted an approach to Dr James Murray about modifying the beta-solenoid, which we would send after iGEM if further wet lab funding is secured:

Overall, we would be testing three chassis as scale-up options, with the remaining two being E. coli at large scale, proposed by Professor Salvador Ventura in a later interaction, and Podospora anserina, the original host of HET-s. The latter would likely possess cellular machinery and pathways optimal for our construct expression, albeit lacking a defined toolbox.

The development of a P. anserina toolbox could build upon our project and parts collection. Deeper exploration of this potential chassis could be valuable not only for prion research but also for senescence, selfish genetic elements, apoptosis, and lignocellulose valourisation studies. Lignocellulose valourisation is also very prominent in our project and could be further expanded upon through exploring the immobilisation and purification of laccases sensu stricto subfamily, native to P. anserina instead of CotA laccase derived from Bacillus subtilis, which is what we used.

items.title: Harry Macpherson
items.body:
Materials scientist, Deep Science Ventures
Sustainability

About them
Harry Macpherson is a materials scientist who previously worked in materials R&D, currently specialising in carbon capture as part of Deep Science Ventures (DSV), working closely with a company Yama he spun out of DSV. Harry authored a toxicity report in collaboration with the Grantham Foundation. The report discusses chemical pollution as a global health emergency, comparing its impacts to climate change. Harry’s goal is to detoxify the economy, reducing the use of persistent chemicals and other dangerous chemical pollutants.

Why we asked
We pursued a conversation with Harry following our interaction with Henrik Hagemann where we discussed the importance of defining a specific market to fill, a “hot” issue demanding a solution. Henrik suggested we speak to Harry regarding the toxicity report he authored, focusing on the demand for non-petrol based materials. We wanted to understand from Harry whether there is a greater demand for biomaterials, particularly those with robustness comparable to non-biological materials, which is what we intended our hydrogel to be. Having researched Harry’s background in entrepreneurship and venture creation, we decided to also consult him about our project’s entrepreneurship and commercialisation.

The conversation
After telling Harry about our project, the conversation directed itself toward applications and identifying the selling point of our hydrogel. Naturally, we spoke about enzyme immobilisation; a concern we raised with Harry that immobilising enzymes on a hydrogel, despite reducing the need for their purification for every reaction, could reduce catalytic efficiency and thus, attractiveness in the industrial biocatalysis field. Harry suggested a different success metric for us, focusing more on increasing enzymatic lifetime and stability and accepting activity loss as a fair tradeoff.

We next spoke about the shift away from petrol-based and environmentally persistent materials. Harry shared his belief in this shift, as exemplified with PEF, a bio-derived packaging alternative of PET, maintaining most valuable properties of the latter. We asked Harry if he believes biomaterials are the solution and were surprised when he denied this claim. He gave multiple examples of bio-based materials, such as bio-polyethylene or cellophane, that are still persistent and toxic. Harry also mentioned regrettable substitution: a case where companies are focused more on selling their chemical as an alternative to an existing product, even though it has a similar or higher level of toxicity. He proposed a pipeline for us to follow to prevent this scenario.

What it changed
Harry recommended us two strategies contradictory to Rahul Khetan’s advice: 1) Leading with a problem instead of a product and tailoring the product to it. and 2) Focusing on securing early wet lab data on enzymatic lifetime superior to market alternatives, not efficiency. We aligned closer with Rahul’s strategy for project development, as a Foundational Advance project; we also remembered Henrik Hagemann’s advice about avoiding a narrow niche in early development of the product, as per CustoMem’s example. However, we preferred Harry’s suggestion regarding marketing emphasis on prolonged enzymatic lifetime, as we suspected possible decrease in catalysis and did not have the capacity to model immobilised enzyme kinetics within the timeline of iGEM. As a result, we emphasised the increase in enzyme lifetime through immobilisation on our hydrogel matrix in an animation within our project promotion video.

What’s more is we confirmed the market niche proposed by Henrik through Harry’s consultation; we incorporated both this niche and the angle on enzyme immobilisation into conversations with potential sponsors and pitching, securing multiple additional sponsorships including a £1000 donation for the UK/EU Mini Jamboree. We also ensured to avoid claiming that biomaterials are generally a more sustainable alternative to non-biological materials in any further scientific communication, as discredited by Harry. Ultimately, we integrated Harry’s proposed protocol to avoid regrettable substitution into our biosecurity framework, tying it into responsible innovation.

This guideline serves as a foundational biosecurity guidance for projects developing new chemicals, relevant beyond iGEM and for iGEM teams, particularly in villages such as Biomanufacturing, Fashion & Cosmetics, Food & Nutrition, Agriculture, and Bioremediation.

items.title: Dr Ross Cummings
items.body:
Partner, Gill Jennings & Every (IP law)
IP and Law

About them
Dr Ross Cummings is a Partner at Gill Jennings & Every LLP, a firm specialising in intellectual property law. He advises on patents and on the Intellectual Property (IP) considerations involved in turning academic research into companies.

Why we asked
Imperial’s Technology Transfer Office connected us with Dr Cummings to discuss intellectual property and university spinouts. Although we ultimately decided not to pursue IP protection for reGELerate, we wanted to understand how academic innovations are protected and commercialised. That understanding matters for any engineering biology project with real-world applications, and for any team member who might one day take an idea beyond the lab.

The conversation
Dr Cummings’s first and most emphatic point was that the specific details of an invention must not be made public before a patent application has been filed. Any earlier disclosure can undermine the ability to protect it. He explained that a patent is a negative right: it does not grant permission to use an invention, but gives the holder the right to stop others from making, using or selling it without permission.

He then outlined what makes a strong application. It must contain enough information to support the invention, and in our field that generally means wet lab results. It should also be considerably broader than the specific use case or dataset, so that it covers downstream variants and improvements that others would need to license. In return for this protection, the invention is disclosed publicly in enough detail that a skilled person could reproduce it, which is what allows others to build on it freely once the patent expires.

Finally, we discussed ownership. Having multiple inventors is standard, but a single applicant, such as Imperial’s commercialisation arm, is preferred because it makes transferring ownership to a spinout company straightforward. Crucially, he stressed that inventorship is determined by who contributed to the inventive concept, not by who carried out the work.

What it changed
The most immediate change was to our record-keeping. Alongside our Benchling notebook, we began keeping a daily, signed physical lab book recording who contributed what, from ideation through to all lab work. This gives a clear record of each person’s contribution should questions of inventorship ever arise.

More broadly, the conversation was an education for the whole team in the mechanics of patents and technology transfer, and several team members have since begun exploring careers in IP law. Dr Cummings’ inputs have also directly fed into our IP strategy, outlined in this wiki.

We also carried Dr Cummings’s points into later conversations. With Henrik Hagemann, co-founder of Puraffinity, we discussed how rigid inventorship can be in deciding who is and is not credited. Henrik reflected on this personally during our UK/EU Mini Jamboree panel, explaining that only two members of the original 2014 Imperial iGEM team went on to spin their innovation out into Puraffinity.

items.title: Tom Furnival
items.body:
Partner, Mewburn Ellis, patent attorney
IP and Law

About them
Tom Furnival is a Partner at Mewburn Ellis LLP and a chartered patent attorney with 12 years’ experience, coming from a background in physics. We met him through an Intellectual Property (IP) clinic run by the Chartered Institute of Patent Attorneys (CIPA).

Why we asked
Over the Easter break, we signed up for CIPA’s IP clinic to build a working understanding of intellectual property before engaging with Imperial’s Enterprise Lab and Technology Transfer Office (TTO). iGEM is unusually open by design: teams are expected to share their work through the wiki, the Parts Registry and the Grand Jamboree presentation. We therefore sought Mr Furnival’s advice on how these forms of disclosure interact with the possibility of protecting our invention.

The conversation
Mr Furnival began with an overview of what a patent application contains: background literature, a summary of the invention and the specific claims being made. He stressed that an application must be filed before the invention’s first enabling disclosure, and that uploading a part to the iGEM Parts Registry would count as one, as would publishing our wiki.

He clarified what makes a disclosure “enabling”: it is made to someone not bound by confidentiality, and it contains enough technical information that someone working in the field (the notional “person skilled in the art”) could reproduce or implement the invention without undue burden. Because external advisers are under no obligation of confidentiality, he recommended that any pre-filing discussions with them be covered by non-disclosure agreements (NDAs).

He then outlined the patent process itself. The UK operates a first-to-file system, and to be patentable an invention must be new and involve an inventive step (be non-obvious), while the application must disclose it in sufficient detail. An initial application typically costs £8,000 to £10,000. After a UK filing, applicants have 12 months to file abroad, at roughly £5,000 per country. Alternatively, an international (PCT) application defers the decision on individual countries until 30 months from the original UK priority date. Finally, he recommended we contact the TTO and Enterprise Lab to clarify the rules around Imperial’s student exemption.

What it changed
The clinic was a valuable introduction to patents and IP for the whole team. We presented our findings to the team and discussed how to balance confidentiality against communicating our project to sponsors and stakeholders, many of whom would benefit from its technical specifics.

Following Mr Furnival’s advice, we contacted Imperial’s TTO to clarify the unusual status of innovations developed through iGEM. This in turn led us to reach out to former Imperial iGEM members Henrik Hagemann and Ben Reeve, who spun their 2014 project out into Puraffinity, to learn from their experience of taking an iGEM project through to a company. Ultimately, we had an option to apply for a patent and enter a “patent pending” stage before the wiki publication. However, we chose to postpone this step outside of iGEM’s scope, as maintaining non-disclosure about central aspects of our project’s science would make advisory support difficult and require us to collect many non-disclosure agreements (NDAs). This decision was also influenced by Henrik Hagemann’s advice during the UK/EU Mini Jamboree panel, suggesting that disclosing the core of the project is not an issue but very likely a benefit, using Puraffinity as an example. Moreover, we did not have sufficient funds to seriously consider a patent application. Nonetheless, our interaction with Mr Furnival was yet another crucial factor towards streamlining our future IP strategy. Finally, we did create an NDA document for our project, which can be used by us in the future or any other iGEM team willing to seriously consider spin out and consequent intellectual property protection.

items.title: Danielle Hamm
items.body:
Director, Nuffield Council on Bioethics
Bioethics

About them
Danielle Hamm has been the director of Nuffield Council on Bioethics (NCOB) since 2021. She works at the intersection of bioethics and governance, promoting critical discussion and decision-making around controversial topics in life sciences, such as assisted dying or IVF.

Why we asked
We emphasised responsibility in our project from its start and the early days of reGELerate’s human practices. With a desire to build our project around an ethical framework, we began writing the ethical handbook, both to map out the chief ethical components surrounding scientific knowledge and engineering biology and to better understand the ethics behind our project. Into this handbook, we aimed to integrate the perspectives of different bioethicists spanning academia, governance, and industry. We wanted to speak to Danielle specifically to gain insights into ethical work in governance and grand scale change it can spearhead.

The conversation
In our conversation, Danielle described the NCOB as a horizon-scanning organisation with multidisciplinary involvement considering the potential ethical implications of emerging science and advising governance, funding, and regulation. When we shared that we felt there is a lack of trust in engineering biology, she asked us for evidence, which turned out to be anecdotal. A discussion on trust followed: Danielle identified purposes behind science, transparency and work reflecting societal values and serving the good of the public as key factors determining trust. When asked where the line is drawn between ambitiously presenting iGEM projects and significantly overstating the truth, she advised to be ambitious but open and to openly acknowledge the applicational versatility of a platform technology, like our hydrogel. She suggested that we should rely on diverse voices to shape the applications pursued.

When asked about strategies used by the NCOB to resolve cases where public and expert opinions clash, Danielle highlighted that such disagreements are very rare, providing multiple examples, such as the Council’s work on genome editing in farm animals, where the public, encompassing members with variables levels of expertise, produced profound discussion comparable to expert-level. The clash is often avoidable if the deliberation is run well. Three useful and contrasting examples Danielle shared are GM crops controversies against the mitochondrial donation and the Precision Breeding Act. The former exemplifies late engagement, lagging behind the spread of misinformation resulting in greater public mistrust. Conversely, the latter two cases demonstrate how early engagement can effectively enable policy to reflect public values in the context of new technologies. Danielle valued critical thinking but cautioned against the ‘deficit model’, the assumption that if the public understood the science they would agree with scientists. Understanding helps people engage critically, but it does not follow that better-informed publics will reach the same conclusions.

items.title: Danielle Hamm, continued
items.body:
Overall, Danielle argued anticipation and early engagement are the most effective tools to ensure governance reflects public values rather than colliding with them. Through early predictions and ethical analysis combined with public dialogue, governance can effectively match societal values and produce critically sound policies. Another interesting point Danielle made is about public dialogue; NCOB establishes effective public dialogue through rigorous recruitment, information balance and planning. Looking at our high school workshops, she suggested there is a need for more accessible resources to establish public dialogue. Furthermore, we asked Danielle whether publicly funded research should come with ethical obligations upon commercialisation. While NCOB has not considered this deliberately, she suggested that the ethical requirements should remain independent from funding sources and that ethical frameworks must be constructed simultaneously with the science. As a final point, Danielle tied back to the importance of anticipation: science frequently outpaces ethical and legal consideration, leading to fallout with public values.

What it changed
Being positioned towards the end of our project, it was very satisfying to see that we have already considered many of key takeaways arising from our conversation with Danielle. Trust is an important component in our project and transparency is something we are heavily prioritising in our wiki write up. Additionally, we had adopted the approach Danielle proposed regarding ambitious project framing. Early anticipation is exemplified by our Integrated Human Practices and Education: we have been reaching out to a diverse pool of stakeholders and communicating both our project and general engineering biology to the public since reGELerate’s early days. Given that the project is still at a nascent stage, the only steps we would need to take are continuing this committed, broad and responsible public outreach. We have also ensured to let the stakeholders’ opinions shape our applications, as evident from multiple interviews in our programme. Our conversation with Danielle also clarified the role of our educational resources. Each is aimed at the very same accessible public dialogue she described, dialogue that allows public values to shape how new technologies develop, rather than responding to them afterwards.

Importantly, Danielle’s insights have synthesised what we have been doing into a clear objective, early anticipation and engagement across many perspectives, providing clear ethical reasons for the importance of this work. Moreover, they have acted as an indispensable input for our ethical handbook, allowing us to clearly outline the role played by governing bodies in ethical framework construction and enabling new technologies to become trustworthy.

items.title: Dr Amritpal Singh
items.body:
Postdoc, Imperial; iGEM Technology Committee
iGEM

About them
Dr Amritpal Singh is a postdoctoral researcher at Imperial College London and a Non-Model Organism Lead on the iGEM Technology Committee. His current research focuses on the use of non-model microbes for bioremediation applications and biomaterial development. Dr Singh is also a former iGEM judge, with profound knowledge of the competition and its interface with our world.

Why we asked
Following the launch of our social media campaign, a LinkedIn post announcing the concept behind our project, Dr Singh kindly reached out and offered support, should we require it. We then sought his iGEM, outreach and scientific research expertise in multiple areas of our project, particularly our wet lab, integrated human practices, and entrepreneurship.

The conversation
Dr Singh attended multiple of our team meetings and some of our team members met him separately for advice. A critical insight Dr Singh immediately shared with us after listening to our project presentation was lacking some canon elements of an iGEM project. He proposed including more design-build-test-learn cycles and, crucially, perform a set of cloning experiments. This would be required to confirm the standardisation of our genetic constructs, a validation for the iGEM Registry of Standard Biological Parts.

We also discussed scaling our project, with Dr Singh suggesting for us to reach out to nfin (formerly Change Bio) and connecting us to Dr Noah Sprent. He encouraged us to consider Komagatoella phaffi as a scale-up chassis. He also encouraged us to seek a sponsorship from nfin bio and run a do a bioreactor run for a construct redesigned for K. phaffi. Moreover, Dr Singh explained to us the steps required to convert a bacterial construct into a eukaryotic, K. phaffi construct. Namely, he introduced to us the concept of codon optimisation and explained how it can be done.

Another aspect of the project we discussed with Dr Singh was marketing strategy. He proposed the following phrasing for our product in presentations: “Modular platform for functional biomaterial development.”. We also spoke about getting involved with accelerators, such as Nucleate UK, to build a network for future commercialisation. We had a brief discussion on intellectual property, where Dr Singh recommended us to use a licensable royalty business model, which still gives leeway for some open science, whilst maintaining a balance with our commercial interests. Finally, Dr Singh was very kind to provide us with helpful advice on iGEM judging criteria, wiki writing, and making the distinction between public outreach and integrated human practices.

What it changed
We would not be exaggerating when Dr Singh saved us from sinking our chances to win a medal in iGEM by pinpointing the essentiality behind cloning experiments and biological part validation. We ended up reaching out to Dr Sprent from nfin bio and designing constructs, forming the foundation of our scale-up strategy. We effectively applied Dr Singh’s proposed phrasing for marketing our product in future pitches, such as our live pitch to Thermo Fisher Scientific representatives, securing us an in-kind sponsorship highly beneficial to the project’s wet lab component. As per Dr Singh’s advice, we connected with Nucleate UK and competed in a biomaterials hackathon, Materialhack, winning our track. As a result, we certainly integrated into Nucleate’s network, connecting with many exciting stakeholders, including Dr Sonja Billerbeck and Kyle Jonsson, who, together with Dr Singh, became the judges for the iGEM project pitches during our UK/EU Mini Jamboree. We are planning to seek Kyle’s support with presentation coaching, as he has prominent experience in this aspect of entrepreneurship, given his role in Nucleate UK as a Hackathon Lead. Competing in Materialhack was also an educational experience for us, which helped us sharpen our project’s enzymatic applications. You can read more about this experience here. Lastly, three of our members sitting on the Synthetic Biology Society Committee took this network beyond iGEM and invited Dr Singh to present at an event they helped organise, introducing synthetic biology to undergraduate and postgraduate students.

nodes.title: Planning and organisation
nodes.body: How can we engage with iGEM teams before the Grand Jamboree? Online meetings were an option, but live conversation matters for everyone’s project. We built on last year’s Imperial team, Growf, who used the Mini Jamboree as a practice ground for team presentations. We set three objectives.
nodes.name: Planning and organisation

nodes.title: 1. Spark discussion

nodes.title: Dr Szymon Manka, our PI
nodes.body:
Opening
He urged teams to ask, before they build, what problem they solve, who benefits and what the downstream effects are, because ethical omissions left alone grow over time. The field needs people who build not only cleverly but wisely.
What we took from itWe took this responsibility seriously from day one.
nodes.name: Dr Szymon Manka, our PI

nodes.title: Professor Tom Ellis
nodes.body:
Keynote
He spoke about engineered living materials. When he discussed bags made with synthetic biology, he asked whether it was a worthy use of effort and answered with numbers, since textiles produce more greenhouse gas than aviation and shipping combined. He also told us about Puraffinity, a company that started as an iGEM project.
What we took from itHis point that biomaterials should be durable yet disassemblable led us to explain reversible crosslinking by biotin displacement on this wiki and in our promotional video.
nodes.name: Professor Tom Ellis

nodes.title: Eight-minute pitches and questions
nodes.body:
Pitches and mini judging
We kept pitches to 8 minutes to mirror the 10 minutes of judging at the Grand Jamboree. This was the part that mattered most to us.
• UCL’s Shellter showed a clean loop: talk to stakeholders, change the design, then check the impact with more interviews. That shaped our four-part interview format.
• CatPURR from Bochum stated their science’s problems clearly, and the judges praised it. We do the same, in line with Sir Paul Nurse’s self-scepticism.
• AntiBioWars from Aix-Marseille raised nickel leaching from a His-tag laccase matrix. See our safety page.
What judges asked usWho would use the hydrogel, and why does it matter? How would we make it cheaply, and why is it better or more sustainable? Both fed our market analysis.
nodes.name: Eight-minute pitches and questions

nodes.title: Kyle Jonsson, Nucleate UK
nodes.body:
After judging
He called the idea strong and told us to pitch as a funnel: a big societal problem, then the specific problem, then our fix, with one slide comparing current hydrogels tied to one application.
What we took from itOur promotional video is a Shark Tank episode in which other hydrogels pitch and are turned down, before reGELerate pitches. He also offered a pitch run-through in early November.
nodes.name: Kyle Jonsson, Nucleate UK

nodes.title: The future of synthetic biology
nodes.body:
Panel
The panel covered the trajectory of the field, shifts in direction, barriers to translation, patenting, misuse, AI and misinformation. They agreed that price decides whether a product enters a market.
What we took from itDr Ledesma-Amaro’s point that a costly scaffold must justify its price by versatility pushed us to put enzyme immobilisation first. Henrik Hagemann advised building patent families around what is published on the wiki, which steered us away from filing. How we decided on IP.
nodes.name: The future of synthetic biology

nodes.title: Connie O’Donnell, bit.bio
nodes.body:
Keynote
She gave four questions for anyone commercialising science. Who will buy it, what do their purchases look like, is there room to grow into nearby problems, and why is it different? Her advice for a spin-out was to stay solvent first.
What we took from itA second commercial framework beside Hilary Sherman’s. It reinforced our focus on enzyme immobilisation and cheaper access. See the market analysis.
nodes.name: Connie O’Donnell, bit.bio

nodes.body: Dr Amritpal Singh closed the day by summing up the judges’ advice for every team: run one narrative through the whole pitch and show lab data.

nodes.body: Presenting in ten minutes forced us to decide what matters most in our project and what can be left out. Hearing the judges' questions to other teams showed us what they look for, especially in the modelling, and which gaps they notice first. Seeing how other teams approached similar problems gave us ideas for our own work. The talks and the panel gave us a broader view of where synthetic biology is being applied. We also made contacts with people from other teams that we plan to follow up.The main lesson is to prepare the modelling section so that it can be explained clearly in a couple of minutes, with its assumptions and limits stated. We will also rehearse our presentation with timed run-throughs and practise answering questions from people outside the team. We will apply this to our own presentation before the final jamboree. nodes.title: RWTH Aachen Aachen iGEM
nodes.body: At the end of August, on the 24th, part of our team traveled to London to attend the UK & EU Mini Jamboree. The Meet Up featured keynote talks on synthetic biology, as well as a Synbio fireside panel that discussed careers and companies in bioengineering and the future of synthetic biology. It gave us an opportunity to present Adesonica outside of Germany and celebrated the international character of iGEM! We were fascinated with the ideas from teams all over the UK and Europe. The feedback we received from fellow iGEM teams and experienced judges directly influenced how we want to present our project at the Grand Jamboree.

nodes.title: Edinburgh iGEM
nodes.body: As the Edinburgh iGEM team we really enjoyed the Imperial Mini Jamboree. The panel discussion was super interesting and covered synthetic biology research, careers in the biotech industry and the ethical side of our work. What we valued most though was getting to talk to other teams. We had some great conversations about the things we'd all been struggling with, like experiments not going to plan, finding funding and keeping on top of human practices alongside lab work. It was really encouraging to hear how other teams had worked through these and it gave us a fresh perspective on our own project. Thanks so much to Imperial iGEM for organising such a great day!
nodes.name: Edinburgh iGEM

nodes.title: Sheffield iGEM
nodes.body: In August, the Sheffield iGEM team took part in the mini-jamboree hosted by Imperial. As the only therapeutics team there, we enjoyed seeing the range of projects from teams across Europe. The three invited speakers, all former iGEM participants now established in synthetic biology, gave us an invaluable chance to ask how they built their careers and where they see the field heading. The judges’ questions were just as useful. They focused on the core ideas of our project, showing us that we had gone into methods and results without first explaining the foundations clearly enough. This helped us understand how to improve our presentation for the Jamboree in November. Overall, we came away with a clearer story to tell, a broader view of the field and much more confidence going into November. Thank you to Imperial iGEM for organising such a welcoming and useful event!

nodes.body:
A two-day biomaterials hackathon with two tracks. We chose the blue sky track, about designing biomaterials for waste valourisation, and won it against a largely postgraduate field.
Four of us and one student we met there built MoYster, a biomimetic water purification system with several material assemblies, inspired by the Billion Oyster Project. A single oyster can purify over 160 litres of water a day.
In effect we ran a microscale iGEM: ideation, modelling, problem definition, market analysis, prototype design, costing, feasibility and revenue, a website and a pitch to judges. It sharpened how we explain our dry lab to people who have not met its maths.

nodes.title: The human practices loop
nodes.body: Dr Sonja Billerbeck asked who owns the water we would purify, and what regulations apply. Our answer, a service for property owners, was improvised, and the question stayed with us. We had thought about application in technical terms only. We then spoke to Edward You, Kirstin Matthews and Danielle Hamm, and stepped away from direct environmental deployment. The biosecurity framework records release as the dominant risk of the laccase application. We invited Dr Billerbeck to judge at our Mini Jamboree.
nodes.name: The human practices loop

nodes.body:
At Metric, the Imperial student bar, we co-hosted a mixer under the Synthetic Biology Society with seven others: Biochemistry, Biology, Computational Biology, Psychoactive Substance Research, Ageing, Entrepreneurship and Bioengineering. About 65 students came, and many said it was their first time hearing about iGEM or synthetic biology outside a lecture.
Synthetic biology meets biochemistry, computation, engineering, policy and economics, yet students from those fields rarely share a room. We made the field part of the atmosphere: drinks labelled with DNA, bacteria and plasmid stickers that opened conversations, a 3D-printed iGEM logo as the centrepiece, and a live DJ.
nodes.name: text

nodes.title: What it changed
nodes.body:
Danielle Hamm told us to anticipate early: find the hopes and worries people hold while a technology is still being developed. The mixer was a small way to try that. Her conversation is listed above.

Gene drives for malaria came up often, with the question of who would release engineered mosquitoes and who is responsible afterwards. Our biosecurity and IP work asks the same question about our own gel. Once we sell the scaffold, responsibility moves to the buyer, who must respect the agreement. It also helped us write formal and street interview questions.

nodes.title: Public interview series
nodes.body: Our product is for companies and labs, not the public. We still wanted to hear from average citizens, to anticipate their concerns, to keep the public open as a future customer, and to learn how education could help. We held 10 interviews around Leicester Square, Soho Square and Piccadilly Circus in central London, where the mix of people is as varied as anywhere.
nodes.name: Public interview series

nodes.title: Synthetic biology is unfamiliar
nodes.body: Most had never heard the term. Associations were usually negative, such as bioweapons or injections, though a few saw progress. After an explanation using alternative protein, people relaxed and many would try it. One person objected to anything “not natural”, which points to teaching the shared basics of life.
nodes.name: Synthetic biology is unfamiliar

nodes.title: Few read the label
nodes.body: Most do not check ingredients, so opinions form from something other than the facts on the pack.
nodes.name: Few read the label

nodes.title: Schools left people unprepared
nodes.body: Respondents of many ages said school had not taught them to judge biotechnology or AI. One suggested art and theatre as a way to communicate, citing plays about dementia.
nodes.name: Schools left people unprepared

nodes.body:
Where the loop closed
We learned that framing and familiarity matter more than technical information, which shaped our ethics handbook. A suggestion to use art became a trading card collection with Ruhr-University Bochum. The finding that education should build familiarity and not only deliver data matches what Sir Paul Nurse and Danielle Hamm told us, and it changed how we structure workshops.

nodes.title: What it showed, and what we changed
nodes.body:
A smaller market with strong differentiation beats a larger market with little. We scored the enzyme immobilisation market this way, which helped us narrow our applications commercially.

What we changed
Hilary saw a gap for ordered, controlled synthetic hydrogels, but we did not sell reGELerate as a precisely defined platform. Matrigel’s value lies in complex signals that a purely synthetic system struggles to copy, our control over the system was still uncertain, and platforms mostly succeed inside large companies. We invested in several applications instead of one.

nodes.title: Disclosure traps
nodes.body: The Registry, the wiki and the Grand Jamboree all count as public disclosure. So do an adviser chat, a pitch, a poster, a post, a Mini Jamboree talk, or a draft wiki page that others can see. You cannot prepare an application and file after the wiki freeze. Filing must come first.

nodes.title: Inventorship is not ownership
nodes.body: Running the experiments does not make you an inventor. Contribution to the inventive idea does. One owner, such as the university, is easier to move into a spin-out. We kept a signed, dated paper lab book next to our electronic one as evidence.
nodes.name: Inventorship is not ownership

nodes.title: What to protect

nodes.title: Why we chose not to file
nodes.body:
• Advice would have slowed down, because keeping the science confidential means NDAs with many advisers, and openness gave us fast help.
• A first filing of £8,000 to £10,000 was out of reach for our budget. Imperial’s Tech Transfer Office could pay, but with conditions under its IP policy.
• Henrik Hagemann’s bet worked for Puraffinity. He disclosed the core, expected the field to grow around it and sought value in applications.
One of our team has since started exploring a career in IP law.
nodes.name: Why we chose not to file

nodes.title: IP checklist for iGEM teams
nodes.body:
• Start signed, dated physical and electronic notebooks.
• Ask a domain expert where the novelty lies.
• Ask your university about ownership rules and student exemptions.
• Book an IP clinic session with a patent attorney.
• Decide as a team whether to file, keep parts confidential or stay open.
• If filing, get signed NDAs before technical talks.
• Hold back wiki, Registry and conference details until filing is done.
• Note the deadlines that follow the priority date.
• Think about the business model, such as licensing.

nodes.title: Why bio-based does not mean safe
nodes.name: Why bio-based does not mean safe

nodes.body:
Harry Macpherson, a materials scientist at Deep Science Ventures, surprised us by denying that biomaterials are the answer. Bio-polyethylene and cellophane, he pointed out, are still persistent and toxic. Regrettable substitution is when a company sells a chemical as an alternative to an existing product even though its toxicity is similar or higher.
He proposed a pipeline to prevent that. It is now part of our biosecurity framework, and it is useful for any project developing new chemicals, especially in biomanufacturing, fashion and cosmetics, food, agriculture and bioremediation.
Read the conversation with Harry Macpherson
nodes.name: text

nodes.body:
What it changed
We stopped claiming that biomaterials are generally more sustainable than non-biological materials in anything we publish. And we pitched enzyme lifetime, not efficiency, since we could not model immobilised kinetics within iGEM. An animation in our promotional video shows the gain in lifetime.

nodes.title: Producing the gel at scale
nodes.body: Protein purification is the main cost bottleneck. Dr Noah Sprent of nfin bio warned us that HET-s may aggregate inside Pichia (K. phaffii), turn toxic and fail to secrete. A kill curve would tell us quickly whether it does.
nodes.name: Producing the gel at scale

nodes.title: What we did
nodes.body: We generated kill curve predictions and outreach drafts, and we codon-optimised three constructs for the pPICZα A vector. These are wild-type HET-s, the tetramer seed and the 1.5-unit cap. They are RFC[10] compatible and ready to order. We have not tested them, so they are not in the Registry.
nodes.name: What we did

nodes.title: What we did not do
nodes.body: The test needed redesigned constructs and a beta-solenoid change, and Dr Sprent’s advice came late in the wet lab timeline. The experiment stays on the roadmap.
nodes.name: What we did not do

nodes.title: Three hosts to compare
nodes.body: K. phaffii, E. coli at large scale as Professor Salvador Ventura suggested, and Podospora anserina, the original host of HET-s. A toolbox for P. anserina could help prion, senescence and lignocellulose research.
nodes.name: Three hosts to compare

nodes.body: Read the conversation with Noah Sprent

nodes.body:
The cell-free gel has no biological waste. What remains depends on what it held. HET-s fibrils resist heat and protease, so we ask for a defined waste route, and the biotin switch gives a gentle way to take the network apart before disposal.
Fibril persistence in waste is the main concern for the cellulosome application. For the laccase gel, adsorbed aromatics and leached copper need a dye-waste route.

nodes.title: Understand
nodes.body:
Pillar 1
The biological risks faced today and those that could emerge.
nodes.name: Understand

nodes.title: Prevent
nodes.body:
Pillar 2
Stop risks emerging, or from threatening the UK and its interests.
nodes.name: Prevent

nodes.title: Detect
nodes.body:
Pillar 3
Characterise and report risks as early and reliably as possible.
nodes.name: Detect

nodes.title: Respond
nodes.body:
Pillar 4
Lessen the impact of risks that arrive, and return to normal quickly.
nodes.name: Respond

nodes.body: Edward You’s argument was that biological material is open-source, dual-use and increasingly handled at bench scale, so surveillance of infrastructure will not govern it. Governance works when design, documentation and distribution sit inside a clear framework. Two features of our gel shape ours.
